# Summary

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) after a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is associated with a lower risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), whereas delayed treatment is associated with higher conversion risk and greater disability accrual. Evidence from early interferon‑beta trials in CIS shows relative risk reductions of roughly 40–50% for progression to CDMS over short follow‑up, with sustained benefits in longer‑term extensions. Reviews and clinical summaries consistently support early treatment in high‑risk CIS patients, particularly those with MRI features of dissemination in space and time, to reduce conversion and neurologic damage.

# What the evidence shows

- Interferon beta (IFNβ) trials in CIS demonstrated that early treatment significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by about 44–50% compared with no immediate treatment, and follow‑up extension studies showed continued reductions (≈35–37%) in conversion risk with early versus delayed therapy. These trials also showed improvements in MRI measures of disease activity with early IFNβ. <cite id="21485162">Early treatment of CIS patients with standard IFNβ significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by 44 to 50%, and 5‑year extension studies confirmed a 35 to 37% reduction in conversion risk with early versus delayed treatment; early IFNβ also delayed progression to CDMS and improved MRI outcomes</cite> <cite id="24494633">In CIS, initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide) following the first attack has been shown to delay conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Initiation of interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate after an initial MS‑like event in CIS has been associated with delays in progression to clinically definite MS and improvements in MRI damage measures</cite>.

- Multiple reviews of CIS treatment conclude that neurologists should consider initiating DMT as early as possible to favorably influence disease course and delay progression to CDMS, while individualizing therapy based on risk profile and adverse effect tolerance. <cite id="31290079">Conversion rates from CIS to clinically definite MS range roughly 20–75%, and neurologists face the challenge of initiating DMT as early as possible to influence disease course; reviews summarize efficacy, safety, and tolerability of DMTs tested in CIS and their value in delaying progression to CDMS</cite> <cite id="21485162">Following CIS, 38–68% develop CDMS; patients with abnormal MRI (56–88% at high risk) are at high conversion risk; early DMT is recommended for high‑risk CIS patients to prevent axonal damage and slow disability progression</cite> <cite id="15853542">Two interferon‑beta formulations delayed conversion into clinically definite MS in CIS, supporting early initiation to reduce relapses, disability progression, and MRI lesion accumulation</cite>.

- Observational and review data indicate that earlier DMT initiation across MS courses, including CIS, is linked to better outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity, slower disability progression), and that delays in diagnosis and treatment increase the risk of conversion and disability. <cite id="24494633">DMT is more effective when initiated early in MS; in patients without CDMS but with a single MS‑consistent attack (CIS), early DMT delays conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Earlier initiation of DMT in MS is associated with better outcomes; for CIS, early interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate delays progression to CDMS and improves MRI measures</cite> <cite id="24494633">Delays in diagnosis and treatment are associated with poor outcomes, underscoring the importance of early intervention in CIS</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- Compared with delayed treatment, early DMT initiation after CIS is associated with a meaningful reduction in conversion to CDMS (approximately 35–50% relative risk reduction in available trials), particularly in high‑risk patients (e.g., CIS with MRI dissemination in space and time, high lesion burden, brainstem involvement, or evidence of axonal damage). <cite id="21485162">Early IFNβ reduced CDMS risk by 44–50% in short‑term and 35–37% in 5‑year extensions; high‑risk CIS (abnormal MRI, 56–88% at high risk) should receive early DMT</cite> <cite id="31290079">CIS conversion rates of 20–75% motivate early DMT to influence progression</cite>.

- Benefits extend beyond clinical conversion: early therapy reduces MRI lesion accrual and activity and may slow disability progression, whereas delayed treatment allows greater neurologic damage before clinically definite MS establishes. <cite id="24217189">Early DMT in CIS delays progression to CDMS and improves MRI damage measures</cite> <cite id="15853542">Interferon‑beta formulations reduced relapses, disability progression, and MRI lesion accumulation in clinically definite MS and delayed conversion from CIS</cite>.

# Caveats and context

- Not all CIS patients progress to CDMS; treatment decisions should be individualized using prognostic markers (e.g., MRI evidence of dissemination in space and time, lesion load, brainstem/spinal cord location, and markers of axonal injury) to target high‑risk patients most likely to benefit. <cite id="21485162">CIS conversion rates vary widely (38–68%); MRI abnormalities identify high‑risk patients (56–88%); early DMT is most appropriate for high‑risk CIS by McDonald criteria</cite> <cite id="31290079">Choice of DMT should balance efficacy with adverse reaction profile and patient compliance</cite>.

# Bottom line

Yes. data.title: Drug Treatment of Clinically Isolated Syndrome.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) that leads to inflammation, demyelination and ultimately axonal degeneration. In most cases, it is preceded by its precursor, clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) with conversion rates to clinically definite MS (CDMS) of roughly 20-75%. Neurologists are therefore faced with the challenge of initiating a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) as early as possible to favorably influence the course of the disease. During the past 20 years, a multitude of drugs have been incorporated into our therapeutic armamentarium for MS and CIS. Choosing the right drug for an individual patient is complex and should be based not only on the drug's overall efficacy to prevent disease progression but also its specific adverse reaction profile, the severity of individual disease courses and, finally, patient compliance in order to adequately weigh associated risks and benefits. Here, we review the available data on the efficacy, safety and tolerability of DMTs tested for CIS and discuss their value regarding a delay of progression to CDMS.

data.title: [Clinically isolated syndrome: prognostic markers for conversion to multiple sclerosis and initiation of disease-modifying therapy].
data.abstract: Eighty-five percent of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) initially present with a single demyelinating event, referred to as a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) of the optic nerves, brainstem, or spinal cord. Following the onset of CIS, 38 to 68% of patients develop clinically definite MS (CDMS). Clinically silent brain lesions are seen on MRI in 50 to 80% of patients with CIS at first clinical presentation and 56 to 88% of CIS patients with abnormal MRI are at high risk of conversion to CDMS. Axonal damage, that is considered to underlie the development of persistent disability in MS, occurs in the CIS stage. Treatment with disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), that might prevent axonal damage and result in slowing the progression of disability, should be initiated early during the disease course. Clinical trials demonstrated that early treatment of CIS patients with the standard dose of interferon beta (IFNbeta) significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by 44 to 50%. After 5 years of followup, the results of the IFNbeta treatment extension studies confirmed that the risk of conversion to CDMS was significantly reduced by 35 to 37% in patients receiving early treatment compared to that in those receiving delayed treatment. However, not every patient with CIS will progress to CDMS; the IFNbeta treatment is appropriately indicated for CIS patients who are diagnosed with MS by McDonald diagnostic criteria based on MRI findings of dissemination in space and time and are at high risk for conversion to CDMS. Development of more reliable prognostic markers will enable DMTs to be targeted for those who are most likely to benefit.

data.title: Impact of delayed diagnosis and treatment in clinically isolated syndrome and multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive inflammatory disease with several possible clinical courses; before the development of definite MS, some patients may have clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), which is a single attack of neurological symptoms caused by inflammation or demyelination. Disease-modifying treatments (DMTs) have been extensively used for the management of MS, resulting in improvements in the clinical presentation and decreases in MS-associated neurological damage. Earlier initiation of DMT in the course of MS is associated with better outcomes. For patients with CIS, initiation of interferon-beta or glatiramer acetate treatment after an initial clinical event indicative of MS has been associated with delays in the progression to clinically definite MS as well as improvements in measures of neurological damage via magnetic resonance imaging. The initiation of treatment for patients with CIS should be considered, and nurses play a vital role in educating patients about the risks of conversion to MS and the benefits of early DMT.

data.title: Impact of diagnosis and early treatment on the course of multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive inflammatory disease of the central nervous system that results in neurological dysfunction and disability. The initiation of disease-modifying therapy (DMT) early in the course of MS may improve the prognosis for patients with MS and reduce the occurrence of neurological damage. In patients with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), DMT reduces the rate of relapses, reduces the appearance of magnetic resonance imaging markers of disease activity, and slows the course of disability progression. DMT has been shown to be more effective when initiated early in the course of MS. In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS (CDMS), but have had 1 attack of neurological symptoms consistent with MS (ie, clinically isolated syndrome [CIS]), the initiation of DMT (specifically, interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS. Current guidelines have recognized the benefits of early treatment of MS with DMTs. However, there are a number of barriers to implementing early MS treatment. Early diagnosis and treatment of MS can be hindered because patients may delay consulting a physician about their neurological symptoms or may be reluctant to start DMT. Further, even after initiating DMT, continued adherence to treatment is often poor. These delays in treatment and a lack of adherence to treatment are associated with poor patient outcomes. The objectives of this review are to highlight the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of CIS or RRMS and discuss the favorable outcomes associated with early initiation of DMT.
data.venue: The American journal of managed care

data.title: Disease-modifying drugs for the early treatment of multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: The introduction of new immunomodulatory therapies such as, interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate (Copaxone, Teva Pharmaceutical Industries) and mitoxantrone (Ralenova, Wyeth Pharma; Novantrone, Immunex Corp.) has considerably improved the therapeutic options for patients with multiple sclerosis. These agents have been shown to reduce relapse rate, slow down progression of disability and prevent the accumulation of magnetic resonance imaging lesion load in clinically definite multiple sclerosis. Moreover, two formulations of interferon-beta delayed conversion into clinically definite multiple sclerosis in patients with clinically isolated syndromes suggestive of multiple sclerosis. Since axonal damage leading to irreversible neurological disability is already present early at the onset of the disease, immunomodulatory therapy should start as soon as possible. This article reviews the arguments for the early initiation of therapy and provides an overview of clinical studies dealing with the early treatment of multiple sclerosis.

# Summary

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) after a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is associated with a lower risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), whereas delayed treatment is associated with higher conversion risk and greater disability accrual. Evidence from early interferon‑beta trials in CIS shows relative risk reductions of roughly 40–50% for progression to CDMS over short follow‑up, with sustained benefits in longer‑term extensions. Reviews and clinical summaries consistently support early treatment in high‑risk CIS patients, particularly those with MRI features of dissemination in space and time, to reduce conversion and neurologic damage.

# What the evidence shows

- Interferon beta (IFNβ) trials in CIS demonstrated that early treatment significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by about 44–50% compared with no immediate treatment, and follow‑up extension studies showed continued reductions (≈35–37%) in conversion risk with early versus delayed therapy. These trials also showed improvements in MRI measures of disease activity with early IFNβ. <cite id="21485162">Early treatment of CIS patients with standard IFNβ significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by 44 to 50%, and 5‑year extension studies confirmed a 35 to 37% reduction in conversion risk with early versus delayed treatment; early IFNβ also delayed progression to CDMS and improved MRI outcomes</cite> <cite id="24494633">In CIS, initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide) following the first attack has been shown to delay conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Initiation of interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate after an initial MS‑like event in CIS has been associated with delays in progression to clinically definite MS and improvements in MRI damage measures</cite>.

- Multiple reviews of CIS treatment conclude that neurologists should consider initiating DMT as early as possible to favorably influence disease course and delay progression to CDMS, while individualizing therapy based on risk profile and adverse effect tolerance. <cite id="31290079">Conversion rates from CIS to clinically definite MS range roughly 20–75%, and neurologists face the challenge of initiating DMT as early as possible to influence disease course; reviews summarize efficacy, safety, and tolerability of DMTs tested in CIS and their value in delaying progression to CDMS</cite> <cite id="21485162">Following CIS, 38–68% develop CDMS; patients with abnormal MRI (56–88% at high risk) are at high conversion risk; early DMT is recommended for high‑risk CIS patients to prevent axonal damage and slow disability progression</cite> <cite id="15853542">Two interferon‑beta formulations delayed conversion into clinically definite MS in CIS, supporting early initiation to reduce relapses, disability progression, and MRI lesion accumulation</cite>.

- Observational and review data indicate that earlier DMT initiation across MS courses, including CIS, is linked to better outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity, slower disability progression), and that delays in diagnosis and treatment increase the risk of conversion and disability. <cite id="24494633">DMT is more effective when initiated early in MS; in patients without CDMS but with a single MS‑consistent attack (CIS), early DMT delays conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Earlier initiation of DMT in MS is associated with better outcomes; for CIS, early interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate delays progression to CDMS and improves MRI measures</cite> <cite id="24494633">Delays in diagnosis and treatment are associated with poor outcomes, underscoring the importance of early intervention in CIS</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- Compared with delayed treatment, early DMT initiation after CIS is associated with a meaningful reduction in conversion to CDMS (approximately 35–50% relative risk reduction in available trials), particularly in high‑risk patients (e.g., CIS with MRI dissemination in space and time, high lesion burden, brainstem involvement, or evidence of axonal damage). <cite id="21485162">Early IFNβ reduced CDMS risk by 44–50% in short‑term and 35–37% in 5‑year extensions; high‑risk CIS (abnormal MRI, 56–88% at high risk) should receive early DMT</cite> <cite id="31290079">CIS conversion rates of 20–75% motivate early DMT to influence progression</cite>.

<snippet id="32584928">Title: Use of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease: A Review.
Authors: Honigberg, Michael C, Chang, Lee-Shing, McGuire, Darren K et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: JAMA cardiology
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
Recent randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) reduce cardiovascular events in at-risk individuals with type 2 diabetes. Despite these findings, GLP-1RAs are underused in eligible patients, particularly by cardiologists.
OBSERVATIONS
To date, randomized clinical trials of albiglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, and injectable semaglutide have reported favorable cardiovascular outcomes. Most recently approved for clinical use, oral semaglutide has a favorable safety profile and is currently undergoing regulatory evaluation and further study for cardiovascular outcomes. Professional society guidelines now recommend GLP-1RA therapy for cardiovascular risk mitigation in patients with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or multiple ASCVD risk factors, independent of glucose control or background antihyperglycemic therapy (other diabetes medications being used). Additional conditions suitable for GLP-1RA therapy include obesity and advanced chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), for which cardiovascular risk-reducing options are limited. Out-of-pocket costs and secondary advantages (eg, weight loss) may inform shared decision-making discussions regarding potential therapies. GLP-1RA therapy has a favorable safety profile. Its most common adverse effect is gastrointestinal upset, which typically wanes during the early weeks of therapy and may be mitigated by starting at the lowest dose and escalating as tolerated. Depending on baseline glycemic control, sulfonylureas and insulin may need to be decreased before GLP-1RA initiation; without concurrent use of insulin or sulfonylureas, GLP-1RAs are not associated with hypoglycemia. Multidisciplinary follow-up and collaborative care with primary care physicians and/or endocrinologists are important.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
Findings from this review suggest that GLP-1RAs are safe, are well tolerated, and improve cardiovascular outcomes, largely independent of their antihyperglycemic properties, but they remain underused by cardiologists. This review provides a practical resource for cardiologists for initiating GLP-1RAs and managing the therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes and established ASCVD or high risk for ASCVD.</snippet>

<snippet id="31032602">Title: Cardiorenal Outcomes in the CANVAS, DECLARE-TIMI 58, and EMPA-REG OUTCOME Trials: A Systematic Review.
Authors: Kluger, Aaron Y, Tecson, Kristen M, Barbin, Clay M et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Reviews in cardiovascular medicine
Abstract: In this systematic review, we sought to summarize the 3 recent sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) trials (Dapagliflozin Effect on CardiovasculAR Events (DECLARE-TIMI 58), Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study (CANVAS) Program, and Empagliflozin, Cardiovascular Outcomes, and Mortality in Type 2 Diabetes (EMPA-REG OUTCOME)) and to explore the potential causes for their different results. We found that the major adverse cardiovascular event rates per 1000 patient-years for drug and placebo, as well as the corresponding relative risk reductions, were 22.6, 24.2, 7%; 26.9, 31.5, 14%; 37.4, 43.9, 14% for DECLARE-TIMI 58, CANVAS, and EMPA-REG OUTCOME, respectively. DECLARETIMI 58 had the fewest cardiorenal events (across treatment and control arms) and EMPA-REG OUTCOME the most. DECLARE-TIMI 58 used alternative inclusion criterion for baseline renal function (creatinine clearance ≧ 60 mL/min) compared to the other trials (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) > 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 bodysurface area). Therefore, the DECLARE-TIMI 58 study cohort had higher eGFR (mean eGFR 85.2 mL/min/1.73 m 2 compared to 76.5 and 74 in CANVAS and EMPAREG OUTCOME, respectively); this may have caused the difference in results. Additionally contributing to the high event rate in EMPA-REG OUTCOME was the requirement of prior confirmed cardiovascular disease (CVD), resulting in 99.2% of patients with CVD compared to only 65.6% and 40.6% in CANVAS and DECLARE-TIMI 58, respectively (which did not require CVD). In conclusion, there is a need for large-scale studies of SGLT2i with matching inclusion/exclusion criteria and appropriate endpoints to ensure a truly direct comparison of the drugs.</snippet>
<snippet id="31725011">Title: Renoprotective effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and underlying mechanisms.
Authors: Kashihara, Naoki, Kidokoro, Kengo, Kanda, Eiichiro | Year: 2020 | Journal: Current opinion in nephrology and hypertension
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Emerging data have demonstrated that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors prevent cardiovascular events, especially heart failure-associated endpoints. Cardiovascular outcome trials have also suggested their renoprotective effects. One large clinical trial investigated renal primary endpoints and demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors slowed the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). This review summarizes clinical trial data on renal outcomes and discusses potential underlying mechanisms.
RECENT FINDINGS
The EMPA-REG, CANVAS, and DECLARE-TIMI 58 studies revealed that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and concomitantly suggested that these drugs slow the progression of kidney disease in type 2 diabetes. The CREDENCE trial on patients with high-risk type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease demonstrated that canagliflozin treatment reduced the relative risk of a composite outcome, including end-stage kidney disease, serum creatinine doubling, and renal/cardiovascular death, by 30% in these patients. Animal experiments revealed that oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, and tubuloglomerular feedback are underlying renoprotective mechanisms behind SGLT2 inhibitors.
SUMMARY
Recent clinical trials have established the renoprotective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors. Further investigations on mechanisms of these renoprotective effects will provide deeper insights and understanding of pathogenetic properties of DKD.</snippet>
<snippet id="36460429">Title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors as the first universal treatment of chronic kidney disease.
Authors: Sharaf El Din, Usama Abdel Azim, Salem, Mona Mansour, Abdulazim, Dina Ossama | Year: 2022 | Journal: Nefrologia
Abstract: In the last five years, the medical community was astonishingly surprised by the sequential large outcome trials that displayed the renal effects of sodium glucose co-transporter inhibitors (SGLT2Is) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients with or without chronic kidney disease (CKD). This favorable effect was later disclosed in non-diabetic CKD patients. The EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial was the first trial that showed a reduction for the need for dialysis in patients suffering diabetic kidney disease (DKD) by 55%. This figure is double the score achieved by the angiotensin receptor blocker, Losartan, in RENAAL trial. The need for dialysis in DAPA-CKD trial was reduced in diabetic and non-diabetic CKD patients by 33%. The renal-specific composite outcome was reduced by 39% in EMPA-REG trial, 40% in CANVAS study, 47% in DECLARE-TIMI 58 study, 34% in CREDENCE trial, and 44% in DAPA-CKD trial. The greater surprise is the significant favorable effect of SGLT2Is on overall mortality in CKD patients with or without T2DM. Similar survival benefit was not previously encountered with any of the medications used in CKD patients with or without diabetes. In this review, we disclose the results of the DAPA-CKD trial, the CREDENCE trial and those of several cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOT) that used different SGLT2Is and showed that patients with lower eGFR levels may have greater benefit with respect to cardiovascular morbidity than patients with normal kidney function. In addition, we discuss the different mechanisms of action that explain the renal beneficial effects of SGLT2Is.</snippet>

Abstract: Published in 2015, the EMPA-REG cardiovascular outcome trial (CVOT) investigated empagliflozin in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). This agent promotes glycosuria by inhibiting Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 (SGLT2), that is expressed in the first segment of the renal proximal tubule. The study aimed to provide evidence for the drug's cardiovascular (CV) safety, as required by regulatory authorities for newly developed glucose lowering agents (GLA)s. This review focuses on the renal aspect of the large trials investigating SGLT2 inhibitors. We will discuss the populations investigated, the defined renal outcomes and their hierarchy within the trials - all used as a framework to interpret the renal findings and their conclusions. Lastly, we will outline some of the suggested mechanisms underlying the renal protective effects of the inhibitors of SGLT2.</snippet>

data.title: Use of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease: A Review.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Recent randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) reduce cardiovascular events in at-risk individuals with type 2 diabetes. Despite these findings, GLP-1RAs are underused in eligible patients, particularly by cardiologists.
OBSERVATIONS
To date, randomized clinical trials of albiglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, and injectable semaglutide have reported favorable cardiovascular outcomes. Most recently approved for clinical use, oral semaglutide has a favorable safety profile and is currently undergoing regulatory evaluation and further study for cardiovascular outcomes. Professional society guidelines now recommend GLP-1RA therapy for cardiovascular risk mitigation in patients with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or multiple ASCVD risk factors, independent of glucose control or background antihyperglycemic therapy (other diabetes medications being used). Additional conditions suitable for GLP-1RA therapy include obesity and advanced chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), for which cardiovascular risk-reducing options are limited. Out-of-pocket costs and secondary advantages (eg, weight loss) may inform shared decision-making discussions regarding potential therapies. GLP-1RA therapy has a favorable safety profile. Its most common adverse effect is gastrointestinal upset, which typically wanes during the early weeks of therapy and may be mitigated by starting at the lowest dose and escalating as tolerated. Depending on baseline glycemic control, sulfonylureas and insulin may need to be decreased before GLP-1RA initiation; without concurrent use of insulin or sulfonylureas, GLP-1RAs are not associated with hypoglycemia. Multidisciplinary follow-up and collaborative care with primary care physicians and/or endocrinologists are important.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
Findings from this review suggest that GLP-1RAs are safe, are well tolerated, and improve cardiovascular outcomes, largely independent of their antihyperglycemic properties, but they remain underused by cardiologists. This review provides a practical resource for cardiologists for initiating GLP-1RAs and managing the therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes and established ASCVD or high risk for ASCVD.

data.title: Cardiorenal Outcomes in the CANVAS, DECLARE-TIMI 58, and EMPA-REG OUTCOME Trials: A Systematic Review.
data.abstract: In this systematic review, we sought to summarize the 3 recent sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) trials (Dapagliflozin Effect on CardiovasculAR Events (DECLARE-TIMI 58), Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study (CANVAS) Program, and Empagliflozin, Cardiovascular Outcomes, and Mortality in Type 2 Diabetes (EMPA-REG OUTCOME)) and to explore the potential causes for their different results. We found that the major adverse cardiovascular event rates per 1000 patient-years for drug and placebo, as well as the corresponding relative risk reductions, were 22.6, 24.2, 7%; 26.9, 31.5, 14%; 37.4, 43.9, 14% for DECLARE-TIMI 58, CANVAS, and EMPA-REG OUTCOME, respectively. DECLARETIMI 58 had the fewest cardiorenal events (across treatment and control arms) and EMPA-REG OUTCOME the most. DECLARE-TIMI 58 used alternative inclusion criterion for baseline renal function (creatinine clearance ≧ 60 mL/min) compared to the other trials (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) > 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 bodysurface area). Therefore, the DECLARE-TIMI 58 study cohort had higher eGFR (mean eGFR 85.2 mL/min/1.73 m 2 compared to 76.5 and 74 in CANVAS and EMPAREG OUTCOME, respectively); this may have caused the difference in results. Additionally contributing to the high event rate in EMPA-REG OUTCOME was the requirement of prior confirmed cardiovascular disease (CVD), resulting in 99.2% of patients with CVD compared to only 65.6% and 40.6% in CANVAS and DECLARE-TIMI 58, respectively (which did not require CVD). In conclusion, there is a need for large-scale studies of SGLT2i with matching inclusion/exclusion criteria and appropriate endpoints to ensure a truly direct comparison of the drugs.

data.title: Renoprotective effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and underlying mechanisms.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Emerging data have demonstrated that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors prevent cardiovascular events, especially heart failure-associated endpoints. Cardiovascular outcome trials have also suggested their renoprotective effects. One large clinical trial investigated renal primary endpoints and demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors slowed the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). This review summarizes clinical trial data on renal outcomes and discusses potential underlying mechanisms.
RECENT FINDINGS
The EMPA-REG, CANVAS, and DECLARE-TIMI 58 studies revealed that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and concomitantly suggested that these drugs slow the progression of kidney disease in type 2 diabetes. The CREDENCE trial on patients with high-risk type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease demonstrated that canagliflozin treatment reduced the relative risk of a composite outcome, including end-stage kidney disease, serum creatinine doubling, and renal/cardiovascular death, by 30% in these patients. Animal experiments revealed that oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, and tubuloglomerular feedback are underlying renoprotective mechanisms behind SGLT2 inhibitors.
SUMMARY
Recent clinical trials have established the renoprotective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors. Further investigations on mechanisms of these renoprotective effects will provide deeper insights and understanding of pathogenetic properties of DKD.

data.title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors as the first universal treatment of chronic kidney disease.
data.abstract: In the last five years, the medical community was astonishingly surprised by the sequential large outcome trials that displayed the renal effects of sodium glucose co-transporter inhibitors (SGLT2Is) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients with or without chronic kidney disease (CKD). This favorable effect was later disclosed in non-diabetic CKD patients. The EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial was the first trial that showed a reduction for the need for dialysis in patients suffering diabetic kidney disease (DKD) by 55%. This figure is double the score achieved by the angiotensin receptor blocker, Losartan, in RENAAL trial. The need for dialysis in DAPA-CKD trial was reduced in diabetic and non-diabetic CKD patients by 33%. The renal-specific composite outcome was reduced by 39% in EMPA-REG trial, 40% in CANVAS study, 47% in DECLARE-TIMI 58 study, 34% in CREDENCE trial, and 44% in DAPA-CKD trial. The greater surprise is the significant favorable effect of SGLT2Is on overall mortality in CKD patients with or without T2DM. Similar survival benefit was not previously encountered with any of the medications used in CKD patients with or without diabetes. In this review, we disclose the results of the DAPA-CKD trial, the CREDENCE trial and those of several cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOT) that used different SGLT2Is and showed that patients with lower eGFR levels may have greater benefit with respect to cardiovascular morbidity than patients with normal kidney function. In addition, we discuss the different mechanisms of action that explain the renal beneficial effects of SGLT2Is.

data.title: [IMPROVEMENT OF RENAL OUTCOMES WITH SODIUM-GLUCOSE COTRANSPORTER-2 (SGLT2) INHIBITORS].
data.abstract: Published in 2015, the EMPA-REG cardiovascular outcome trial (CVOT) investigated empagliflozin in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). This agent promotes glycosuria by inhibiting Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 (SGLT2), that is expressed in the first segment of the renal proximal tubule. The study aimed to provide evidence for the drug's cardiovascular (CV) safety, as required by regulatory authorities for newly developed glucose lowering agents (GLA)s. Surprisingly, besides being safe, empagliflozin was effective in reducing CV morbidity and mortality as well as improving renal outcomes, compared with placebo. EMPA-REG was followed by subsequent CVOTs that demonstrated the value of additional SGLT2 inhibitors to improve CV and renal outcomes in different populations: patients with mostly normal kidney function (DECLARE-TIMI 58), with early stage chronic kidney disease (CKD) (EMPA-REG and CANVAS) and patients with advanced proteinuric CKD (CREDENCE). Intriguingly, recent reports demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors improve CV and renal outcomes in high-risk populations with and without T2D: patients with CKD (DAPA-CKD) or with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced). This review focuses on the renal aspect of the large trials investigating SGLT2 inhibitors. We will discuss the populations investigated, the defined renal outcomes and their hierarchy within the trials - all used as a framework to interpret the renal findings and their conclusions. Lastly, we will outline some of the suggested mechanisms underlying the renal protective effects of the inhibitors of SGLT2.

<snippet id="32676311">Title: EGFR mutation genotypes affect efficacy and resistance mechanisms of osimertinib in T790M-positive NSCLC patients.
Authors: Zheng, Qiufan, Huang, Yan, Zhao, Hongyun et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Translational lung cancer research
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Osimertinib is a potent third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with robust activity in advanced EGFR -mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including those with T790M resistance mutation. However, a broad interpatient variability was observed. This study aimed to evaluate whether EGFR -mutant genotypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms in T790M-positive NSCLC patients receiving osimertinib therapy.
METHODS
All NSCLC patients treated with osimertinib in our institute were screened. We included those with known EGFR -mutant genotypes and T790M positivity. Clinical outcomes including objective response rate (ORR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS), were evaluated and compared between different EGFR genotypes. Patients with next-generation sequencing testing or tumor rebiopsy after osimertinib treatment were analyzed for resistance mechanisms.
RESULTS
ORR, CBR, PFS, and OS were all non-significantly different among patients harboring EGFR exon 19 deletion (19Del, n=136), L858R (n=93), and uncommon mutations (n=6). However, a subset of tumors with deletion starting at E746 (ΔE746, n=98), but not non-ΔE746 tumors (n=38), had better clinical outcomes than L858R tumors (n=93). Frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib treatment were similar between 19Del (n=56) and L858R tumors (n=33). However, compared with L858R tumors (n=33), those with 19Del ΔE746 subtype (n=40) had a higher whereas non-ΔE746 subtype (n=16) had a similar frequency of acquired C797S mutation. Combined analysis of our cohort and public cohort confirmed these findings.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings indicate that the EGFR 19Del subtypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms to osimertinib in T790M-positive patients. Identifying patients with relatively worse treatment outcomes may be informative for establishing new therapies for these patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="40654861">Title: Complementary modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma through MAPK activation and cellular plasticity.
Authors: Zatzman, Matthew, Quintanal-Villalonga, Alvaro, Salehi, Sohrab et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract: EGFR -mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) represents 20% of all non-small cell lung carcinomas, with most patients presenting with incurable metastatic disease. Treatment with mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) results in initial tumor reduction, yet nearly all patients eventually relapse. The mechanisms driving drug resistance are incompletely understood, creating significant barriers to curing metastatic disease. We integrated clinical genomic and single-nuclei RNA (snRNA) sequencing from a cohort of 62 EGFR -mutant LUAD patients treated with the third generation EGFR TKI, osimertinib, and compared treatment-naïve (TN), minimal residual disease (MRD), and progressive disease (PD) tumors. We found that disease progression is associated with a marked decrease in alveolar lineage fidelity, coincident with reduced MAPK signaling and adenocarcinoma identity. PD tumors with sustained MAPK pathway activity, such as those with EGFR or MET amplifications, tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity. In contrast, MAPK-low tumors were more likely to undergo histological transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages. Remarkably, we observed rare tumor cell populations prior to treatment that were poorly differentiated, in some cases with neuroendocrine or squamous features. At progression, these histologically divergent tumor cells increased in prevalence, both in cases with overt histological transformation, and in others with sub-clinical histological plasticity. These findings suggest that pre-existing capacity for histologic plasticity may be a substrate for therapy induced selection. Taken together, our results illuminate genomically encoded MAPK signaling and lineage plasticity as complementary mechanisms of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma.</snippet>
<snippet id="30228210">Title: Landscape of EGFR-Dependent and -Independent Resistance Mechanisms to Osimertinib and Continuation Therapy Beyond Progression in EGFR -Mutant NSCLC.
Authors: Le, Xiuning, Puri, Sonam, Negrao, Marcelo V et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: PURPOSE
Osimertinib was initially approved for T790M-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and, more recently, for first-line treatment of EGFR -mutant NSCLC. However, resistance mechanisms to osimertinib have been incompletely described.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
Using cohorts from The University of Texas MD Anderson Lung Cancer Moonshot GEMINI and Moffitt Cancer Center lung cancer databases, we collected clinical data for patients treated with osimertinib. Molecular profiling analysis was performed at the time of progression in a subset of the patients.
RESULTS
In the 118 patients treated with osimertinib, 42 had molecular profiling at progression. T790M was preserved in 21 (50%) patients and lost in 21 (50%). EGFR C797 and L792 (26%) mutations were the most common resistance mechanism and were observed exclusively in T790M-preserved cases. MET amplification was the second most common alteration (14%). Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET. Preclinical studies confirmed MET, PIK3CA, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition as potential resistance drivers. Alterations of cell-cycle genes were associated with shorter median progression-free survival (PFS, 4.4 vs. 8.8 months, P = 0.01). In 76 patients with progression, osimertinib was continued in 47 cases with a median second PFS (PFS2) of 12.6 months; 21 patients received local consolidation radiation with a median PFS of 15.5 months. Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with a longer overall survival compared with discontinuation (11.2 vs. 6.1 months, P = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS
Osimertinib resistance is associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR-independent genomic alterations. Continuation of osimertinib after progression, alone or in conjunction with radiotherapy, may provide prolonged clinical benefit in selected patients. See related commentary by Devarakonda and Govindan, p. 6112 .</snippet>

<snippet id="31027702">Title: From the beginning to resistance: Study of plasma monitoring and resistance mechanisms in a cohort of patients treated with osimertinib for advanced T790M-positive NSCLC.
Authors: Bordi, Paola, Del Re, Marzia, Minari, Roberta et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Lung cancer (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for the identification of T790M mutation in advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients can replace tissue re-biopsy for resistance characterization and, being non-invasive, may be applied for disease monitoring. We analysed ctDNA during osimertinib treatment to correlate mutational levels with clinical outcome and to predict pattern of resistance.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Forty patients with advanced NSCLC receiving osimertinib for T790M + disease after previous EGFR-TKI were enrolled in a pilot study to collect plasma at baseline and every 12 weeks until progression. Molecular analysis of ctDNA was performed by ddPCR and Therascreen®. When feasible at progression, tissue re-biopsy and NGS analysis were performed.
RESULTS
Thirty-eight patients had baseline plasma samples suitable for molecular analysis. Patients with low levels of the EGFR activating mutation in ctDNA [< 2200 copies/mL or allele frequency (AF) < 6.1%] showed better progression-free survival (17.8 or 17.8 months vs. 4.3 or 2.7, p = 0.022 or p = 0.018, respectively) and overall survival (23.6 or 23.6 vs. 7.7 or 7.3, p = 0.016 or p = 0.013, respectively) than patients with high levels (≥ 2200 copies/mL or AF ≥ 6.1%). Patients with detectable EGFR mutations in plasma (shedders) presented worse outcome than negative subjects (non-shedders). Low levels of T790M, higher T790M/activating mutation ratio and complete clearance after 2 months were associated with a trend towards better outcome. Tissue re-biopsy at resistance showed 3 patients with EGFR C797S, 1 with MET amplification, 1 with MYC amplification, 1 with PTEN loss, 3 with SCLC transformation.
CONCLUSIONS
The mutational analysis performed on plasma plays a significant role in prognostic stratification, especially for the EGFR activating mutation, since patients with absence or low levels of mutations presented a better outcome to osimertinib. At progression, tissue re-biopsy remains a crucial issue for the identification of resistance mechanisms.</snippet>
<snippet id="31027916">Title: Analysis of resistance mechanisms to abivertinib, a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, in patients with EGFR T790M-positive non-small cell lung cancer from a phase I trial.
Authors: Zhang, Yi-Chen, Chen, Zhi-Hong, Zhang, Xu-Chao et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: EBioMedicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Resistance to third-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) presents a major clinical challenge in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, we report resistance mechanisms to abivertinib, a novel third-generation EGFR TKI, from a phase I dose-escalation/expansion study (NCT02330367).
METHODS
Patients with EGFR T790M-positive advanced NSCLC and progression on prior EGFR TKIs received abivertinib in dose escalation (50-350 mg twice daily [BID]) or expansion (300 mg BID) cohorts. Patients enrolled at Guangdong Lung Cancer Institute who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based genomic profiling upon abivertinib progression (prior to October 30, 2018) were enrolled in this exploratory analysis.
FINDINGS
Thirty of 73 patients enrolled were eligible for resistance analysis. Upon abivertinib progression, 27 patients provided plasma samples (six patients also provided paired samples from the progression sites) and three patients only provided tissue samples from the progression sites for NGS. A heterogeneous landscape of resistance to abivertinib was observed: 15% (4/27) experienced EGFR T790M loss and 13% (4/30) developing EGFR tertiary mutations including C797S. EGFR amplification was observed in 11 patients (37%), and considered a putative resistance mechanism in seven (23%) patients. Other EGFR-independent resistance mechanisms involved CDKN2A, MET, PIK3CA, HER2, TP53, Rb1 and small-cell lung cancer transformation.
INTERPRETATION
Our findings reveal a heterogenous pattern of resistance mechanisms to abivertinib which is distinct from that previously reported with osimertinib. EGFR amplification was the most common resistance mechanism in this cohort. # Summary

In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors (notably osimertinib) most commonly arises through EGFR‑dependent mechanisms (T790M loss and tertiary EGFR mutations such as C797S/L792) and EGFR‑independent alterations (MET amplification, PIK3CA/PTEN/PI3K‑AKT‑MTOR pathway changes, FGFR/RET fusions, and histologic transformation), with frequencies varying by cohort and prior genotype. Across clinical series, EGFR C797 and L792 mutations are the most frequent resistance drivers in T790M‑preserved disease, followed by MET amplification, with additional recurrent events in PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET; non‑oncogenic lineage plasticity and MAPK pathway activity also contribute. Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression can yield prolonged benefit in selected patients.

# EGFR-Dependent Resistance Mechanisms

- T790M loss and tertiary EGFR mutations: In combined analyses, T790M loss and C797S acquisition are frequent and often occur together, particularly in T790M‑preserved cases. One cohort reported T790M loss and C797S acquisition in 50% of cases at progression, with C797S/L792 mutations observed exclusively in T790M‑preserved tumors, and overall comprising the most common resistance alterations in that series. Another study found similar frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib, with ΔE746 19Del tumors showing higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R tumors. In abivertinib‑treated T790M‑positive patients, 15% had T790M loss and 13% developed tertiary EGFR mutations including C797S. <cite id="30228210">EGFR C797 and L792 mutations were the most common resistance mechanism and were observed exclusively in T790M-preserved cases</cite> <cite id="32676311">Frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertininib were similar between exon 19 deletion and L858R tumors, with ΔE746 19Del showing higher acquired C797S frequency</cite> <cite id="31027916">15% (4/27) experienced EGFR T790M loss and 13% (4/30) developed EGFR tertiary mutations including C797S</cite>.

# EGFR-Independent Resistance Mechanisms

- MET amplification: Frequently implicated as a secondary driver, often with lower‑order prevalence than C797S/L792 in some cohorts. One series identified MET amplification as the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), with preclinical data supporting MET as a resistance driver. <cite id="30228210">MET amplification was the second most common alteration (14%) and preclinical studies confirmed MET as a potential resistance driver</cite>.

- PI3K–AKT–MTOR pathway alterations: Common recurrent events include PIK3CA, PTEN loss, and FGFR/RET fusions, which can mediate bypass signaling and resistance. <cite id="30228210">Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET; PTEN loss was also observed, and preclinical studies confirmed PIK3CA and EMT as potential resistance drivers</cite>.

- Lineage plasticity and MAPK signaling: Integrated genomic and single‑nuclei RNA sequencing in osimertinib‑treated patients showed that PD tumors with sustained MAPK activity (e.g., via EGFR or MET amplification) retain adenocarcinoma identity, whereas MAPK‑low tumors undergo histologic transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages; pre‑existing poorly differentiated populations may be selected under therapy. <cite id="40654861">Disease progression was associated with decreased adenocarcinoma identity; PD tumors with sustained MAPK activity (EGFR or MET amplifications) retained adenocarcinoma identity, while MAPK-low tumors underwent histologic transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages; pre-existing poorly differentiated populations expanded at progression</cite>.

data.title: EGFR mutation genotypes affect efficacy and resistance mechanisms of osimertinib in T790M-positive NSCLC patients.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Osimertinib is a potent third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with robust activity in advanced EGFR -mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including those with T790M resistance mutation. However, a broad interpatient variability was observed. This study aimed to evaluate whether EGFR -mutant genotypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms in T790M-positive NSCLC patients receiving osimertinib therapy.
METHODS
All NSCLC patients treated with osimertinib in our institute were screened. We included those with known EGFR -mutant genotypes and T790M positivity. Clinical outcomes including objective response rate (ORR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS), were evaluated and compared between different EGFR genotypes. Patients with next-generation sequencing testing or tumor rebiopsy after osimertinib treatment were analyzed for resistance mechanisms.
RESULTS
ORR, CBR, PFS, and OS were all non-significantly different among patients harboring EGFR exon 19 deletion (19Del, n=136), L858R (n=93), and uncommon mutations (n=6). However, a subset of tumors with deletion starting at E746 (ΔE746, n=98), but not non-ΔE746 tumors (n=38), had better clinical outcomes than L858R tumors (n=93). Frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib treatment were similar between 19Del (n=56) and L858R tumors (n=33). However, compared with L858R tumors (n=33), those with 19Del ΔE746 subtype (n=40) had a higher whereas non-ΔE746 subtype (n=16) had a similar frequency of acquired C797S mutation. Combined analysis of our cohort and public cohort confirmed these findings.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings indicate that the EGFR 19Del subtypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms to osimertinib in T790M-positive patients. Identifying patients with relatively worse treatment outcomes may be informative for establishing new therapies for these patients.

data.title: Complementary modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma through MAPK activation and cellular plasticity.
data.abstract: EGFR -mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) represents 20% of all non-small cell lung carcinomas, with most patients presenting with incurable metastatic disease. Treatment with mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) results in initial tumor reduction, yet nearly all patients eventually relapse. The mechanisms driving drug resistance are incompletely understood, creating significant barriers to curing metastatic disease. We integrated clinical genomic and single-nuclei RNA (snRNA) sequencing from a cohort of 62 EGFR -mutant LUAD patients treated with the third generation EGFR TKI, osimertinib, and compared treatment-naïve (TN), minimal residual disease (MRD), and progressive disease (PD) tumors. We found that disease progression is associated with a marked decrease in alveolar lineage fidelity, coincident with reduced MAPK signaling and adenocarcinoma identity. PD tumors with sustained MAPK pathway activity, such as those with EGFR or MET amplifications, tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity. In contrast, MAPK-low tumors were more likely to undergo histological transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages. Remarkably, we observed rare tumor cell populations prior to treatment that were poorly differentiated, in some cases with neuroendocrine or squamous features. At progression, these histologically divergent tumor cells increased in prevalence, both in cases with overt histological transformation, and in others with sub-clinical histological plasticity. These findings suggest that pre-existing capacity for histologic plasticity may be a substrate for therapy induced selection. Taken together, our results illuminate genomically encoded MAPK signaling and lineage plasticity as complementary mechanisms of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma.

data.title: Landscape of EGFR-Dependent and -Independent Resistance Mechanisms to Osimertinib and Continuation Therapy Beyond Progression in EGFR -Mutant NSCLC.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Osimertinib was initially approved for T790M-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and, more recently, for first-line treatment of EGFR -mutant NSCLC. However, resistance mechanisms to osimertinib have been incompletely described.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
Using cohorts from The University of Texas MD Anderson Lung Cancer Moonshot GEMINI and Moffitt Cancer Center lung cancer databases, we collected clinical data for patients treated with osimertinib. Molecular profiling analysis was performed at the time of progression in a subset of the patients.
RESULTS
In the 118 patients treated with osimertinib, 42 had molecular profiling at progression. T790M was preserved in 21 (50%) patients and lost in 21 (50%). EGFR C797 and L792 (26%) mutations were the most common resistance mechanism and were observed exclusively in T790M-preserved cases. MET amplification was the second most common alteration (14%). Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET. Preclinical studies confirmed MET, PIK3CA, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition as potential resistance drivers. Alterations of cell-cycle genes were associated with shorter median progression-free survival (PFS, 4.4 vs. 8.8 months, P = 0.01). In 76 patients with progression, osimertinib was continued in 47 cases with a median second PFS (PFS2) of 12.6 months; 21 patients received local consolidation radiation with a median PFS of 15.5 months. Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with a longer overall survival compared with discontinuation (11.2 vs. 6.1 months, P = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS
Osimertinib resistance is associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR-independent genomic alterations. Continuation of osimertinib after progression, alone or in conjunction with radiotherapy, may provide prolonged clinical benefit in selected patients. See related commentary by Devarakonda and Govindan, p. 6112 .

data.title: From the beginning to resistance: Study of plasma monitoring and resistance mechanisms in a cohort of patients treated with osimertinib for advanced T790M-positive NSCLC.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for the identification of T790M mutation in advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients can replace tissue re-biopsy for resistance characterization and, being non-invasive, may be applied for disease monitoring. We analysed ctDNA during osimertinib treatment to correlate mutational levels with clinical outcome and to predict pattern of resistance.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Forty patients with advanced NSCLC receiving osimertinib for T790M + disease after previous EGFR-TKI were enrolled in a pilot study to collect plasma at baseline and every 12 weeks until progression. Molecular analysis of ctDNA was performed by ddPCR and Therascreen®. When feasible at progression, tissue re-biopsy and NGS analysis were performed.
RESULTS
Thirty-eight patients had baseline plasma samples suitable for molecular analysis. Patients with low levels of the EGFR activating mutation in ctDNA [< 2200 copies/mL or allele frequency (AF) < 6.1%] showed better progression-free survival (17.8 or 17.8 months vs. 4.3 or 2.7, p = 0.022 or p = 0.018, respectively) and overall survival (23.6 or 23.6 vs. 7.7 or 7.3, p = 0.016 or p = 0.013, respectively) than patients with high levels (≥ 2200 copies/mL or AF ≥ 6.1%). Patients with detectable EGFR mutations in plasma (shedders) presented worse outcome than negative subjects (non-shedders). Low levels of T790M, higher T790M/activating mutation ratio and complete clearance after 2 months were associated with a trend towards better outcome. Tissue re-biopsy at resistance showed 3 patients with EGFR C797S, 1 with MET amplification, 1 with MYC amplification, 1 with PTEN loss, 3 with SCLC transformation.
CONCLUSIONS
The mutational analysis performed on plasma plays a significant role in prognostic stratification, especially for the EGFR activating mutation, since patients with absence or low levels of mutations presented a better outcome to osimertinib. At progression, tissue re-biopsy remains a crucial issue for the identification of resistance mechanisms.

data.title: Analysis of resistance mechanisms to abivertinib, a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, in patients with EGFR T790M-positive non-small cell lung cancer from a phase I trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Resistance to third-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) presents a major clinical challenge in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, we report resistance mechanisms to abivertinib, a novel third-generation EGFR TKI, from a phase I dose-escalation/expansion study (NCT02330367).
METHODS
Patients with EGFR T790M-positive advanced NSCLC and progression on prior EGFR TKIs received abivertinib in dose escalation (50-350 mg twice daily [BID]) or expansion (300 mg BID) cohorts. Patients enrolled at Guangdong Lung Cancer Institute who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based genomic profiling upon abivertinib progression (prior to October 30, 2018) were enrolled in this exploratory analysis.
FINDINGS
Thirty of 73 patients enrolled were eligible for resistance analysis. Upon abivertinib progression, 27 patients provided plasma samples (six patients also provided paired samples from the progression sites) and three patients only provided tissue samples from the progression sites for NGS. A heterogeneous landscape of resistance to abivertinib was observed: 15% (4/27) experienced EGFR T790M loss and 13% (4/30) developing EGFR tertiary mutations including C797S. EGFR amplification was observed in 11 patients (37%), and considered a putative resistance mechanism in seven (23%) patients. Other EGFR-independent resistance mechanisms involved CDKN2A, MET, PIK3CA, HER2, TP53, Rb1 and small-cell lung cancer transformation.
INTERPRETATION
Our findings reveal a heterogenous pattern of resistance mechanisms to abivertinib which is distinct from that previously reported with osimertinib. EGFR amplification was the most common resistance mechanism in this cohort. <snippet id="39290529">Title: Hemorrhagic complications after stroke treatment with intravenous thrombolysis despite use of direct oral anticoagulants: an observational study.
Authors: Kleeberg, Antonia, Ringleb, Peter A, Huber, Ioana et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Therapeutic advances in neurological disorders
Abstract: BACKGROUND
For patients experiencing ischemic stroke despite receiving therapy with direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) and without endovascular treatment options, therapeutic prospects are currently dismal. Current guidelines recommend intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) only for patients who have received DOAC in very restricted settings, as an increased risk of bleeding is suspected. However, recent retrospective observational studies suggest that IVT is safe despite DOAC pretreatment.
OBJECTIVES
To provide further evidence that IVT despite previous DOAC treatment is not associated with an increased risk of bleeding.
DESIGN
Observational retrospective study.
METHODS
Demographic, clinical, and radiological data of patients who received IVT (+/- endovascular thrombectomy) despite DOAC pretreatment between June 2021 and January 2024 were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including DOAC plasma concentration at admission. Secondary intracranial hemorrhages and functional outcomes at 3 months were assessed. Since 2023, patients have been treated according to a modified local standard operating procedure at our hospital, allowing for IVT despite DOAC pretreatment regardless of DOAC plasma levels or the use of reversal agents.
RESULTS
Of 1821 patients treated with acute recanalization procedures during the study period, N = 35 had received IVT with (18) or without (17) additional endovascular therapy. Among these patients with a wide age range (42-97 years) and DOAC plasma concentrations up to 369 ng/ml, only one developed symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. - SITS International Stroke Registry (Ann Neurol, 2025): This propensity-matched analysis compared 894 DOAC patients to 1,788 no-OAC patients receiving IV thrombolysis. - Single-center observational study (Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders, 2024): IVT was administered to 35 patients with prior DOAC exposure (age 42–97; DOAC plasma concentrations up to 369 ng/mL) under a modified SOP allowing IVT regardless of DOAC levels or reversal. data.title: Hemorrhagic complications after stroke treatment with intravenous thrombolysis despite use of direct oral anticoagulants: an observational study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
For patients experiencing ischemic stroke despite receiving therapy with direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) and without endovascular treatment options, therapeutic prospects are currently dismal. Current guidelines recommend intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) only for patients who have received DOAC in very restricted settings, as an increased risk of bleeding is suspected. However, recent retrospective observational studies suggest that IVT is safe despite DOAC pretreatment.
OBJECTIVES
To provide further evidence that IVT despite previous DOAC treatment is not associated with an increased risk of bleeding.
DESIGN
Observational retrospective study.
METHODS
Demographic, clinical, and radiological data of patients who received IVT (+/- endovascular thrombectomy) despite DOAC pretreatment between June 2021 and January 2024 were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including DOAC plasma concentration at admission. Secondary intracranial hemorrhages and functional outcomes at 3 months were assessed. Since 2023, patients have been treated according to a modified local standard operating procedure at our hospital, allowing for IVT despite DOAC pretreatment regardless of DOAC plasma levels or the use of reversal agents.
RESULTS
Of 1821 patients treated with acute recanalization procedures during the study period, N = 35 had received IVT with (18) or without (17) additional endovascular therapy. Among these patients with a wide age range (42-97 years) and DOAC plasma concentrations up to 369 ng/ml, only one developed symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. A favorable outcome (modified Rankin scale score 0-2) after 3 months was observed in 57% (20) of the patients.
CONCLUSION
IVT despite direct oral anticoagulation seems to be safe, even at advanced age and high DOAC plasma levels.

Abstract: Ex vivo activation is a prerequisite to reaching adequate levels of gene editing by homology-directed repair (HDR) for hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC)-based clinical applications. Here, we show that shortening culture time mitigates the p53-mediated DNA damage response to CRISPR-Cas9-induced DNA double-strand breaks, enhancing the reconstitution capacity of edited HSPCs. Mechanistically, ex vivo activation triggers a multi-step process initiated by p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation, which generates mitogenic reactive oxygen species (ROS), promoting fast cell-cycle progression and subsequent proliferation-induced DNA damage. # Summary

CRISPR-Cas9 editing in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) can activate DNA damage responses and p53-dependent pathways through double-strand breaks (DSBs), leading to cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, or senescence, and shaping clonal selection in favor of cells with repair advantages or tolerance mechanisms. Multiple mechanistic axes have been reported: (1) DSBs trigger canonical ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM)/ATR–Chk2 pathways and p53 activation, producing growth arrest and deletion-prone repair; (2) proliferative stress and ROS downstream of p38 MAPK accelerate cell-cycle transit, increasing replication stress and DNA damage, which biases selection toward faster-dividing clones; (3) p53-driven senescence and inflammatory signaling (e.g., IL‑1/NF‑κB) induce durable senescence-like states that restrict graft size and clonal diversity unless mitigated; and (4) base editing can avoid p53 activation and large deletions compared with Cas9 nuclease, preserving clonal diversity. These mechanisms are supported by studies in HSPCs and related blood cells, and they inform strategies to mitigate genotoxicity while maintaining editing efficiency.

# Mechanisms of p53 Pathway Activation after Cas9 Editing

- Double-strand breaks and ATM/ATR–Chk2–p53 signaling: Cas9-induced DSBs engage the ATM/ATR kinase axis and Chk2, leading to p53 stabilization and activation. This triggers cell-cycle checkpoints, apoptosis, or senescence, and promotes error-prone repair pathways that can yield deletions and chromosomal abnormalities, thereby shaping clonal composition toward cells with advantageous repair outcomes or tolerance of damage. Evidence from HSPCs and other hematologic systems shows that shortening ex vivo culture mitigates p53-mediated DNA damage responses to Cas9-induced DSBs, improving reconstitution, indicating that p53 signaling is a key driver of post-editing dysfunction and selection pressures in HSPCs. <cite id="39536752">Ex vivo activation shortens culture time mitigates the p53-mediated DNA damage response to CRISPR-Cas9-induced DNA double-strand breaks, enhancing reconstitution capacity of edited HSPCs</cite>.

- Proliferation stress, ROS, and checkpoint activation: Ex vivo activation of HSPCs triggers a p38 MAPK–dependent increase in mitogenic reactive oxygen species, accelerating G1/S transition and inducing proliferation-induced DNA damage. This proliferative stress amplifies DSBs and activates p53 pathways, biasing selection toward clones that progress rapidly through the cell cycle despite damage, at the expense of genome integrity. Pharmacologic p38 inhibition delays G1/S, expands quiescent HSCs, and yields edited cells with superior multilineage differentiation, persistence, polyclonal diversity, and preserved genome integrity, directly linking proliferative stress to clonal selection dynamics. <cite id="39536752">Ex vivo activation triggers a p38 MAPK phosphorylation–ROS axis that promotes fast G1/S progression and proliferation-induced DNA damage, and p38 inhibition expands HSCs and improves edited cell persistence and polyclonal repertoire</cite>.

- Senescence and inflammatory signaling downstream of p53: In HSPCs engineered with Cas9/AAV6 via HDR, durable senescence-like responses are observed, driven by p53 and IL‑1/NF‑κB activation. These responses restrict long-term repopulating capacity and reduce clonal diversity, indicating that inflammatory cytokine signaling cooperates with p53 to enforce a senescence program that curbs competitive fitness of edited clones. Temporary p53 inhibition or blocking IL‑1 signaling (e.g., with anakinra) mitigates these responses and improves repopulating capacity and polyclonal output, demonstrating a therapeutic window to reduce p53/IL‑1–mediated selection against edited clones. <cite id="40466639">CRISPR-Cas9/AAV6 editing in HSPCs triggers durable senescence via p53 and IL‑1/NF‑κB activation, limiting repopulation and clonal diversity; transient p53 inhibition or anakinra mitigates senescence and improves repopulating capacity and polyclonality</cite>.

- p53-mediated proliferation delay and off-targets: In patient-derived HSPCs edited for Friedreich ataxia, a p53-mediated proliferation delay is observed without major off-target lesions, consistent with p53-driven growth control being a dominant effect of Cas9 editing. This proliferation delay represents a clonal selection pressure that reduces the expansion of highly damaged or misrepaired cells while allowing survival of cells with tolerable lesions or efficient repair. <cite id="32462051">CRISPR-Cas9 editing of HSPCs from Friedreich ataxia patients induced a p53-mediated proliferation delay in edited cells without major off-target effects</cite>.

# Clonal Selection Outcomes and Mitigation Strategies

- Bias toward proliferative clones and loss of diversity: The p38–ROS–proliferation axis and p53–NF‑κB–senescence program together impose selection pressures that favor rapidly cycling clones and disfavors quiescent, long-term repopulating HSPCs, reducing clonal diversity and grafting efficiency. <cite id="39536752">A p38–ROS–proliferation stress axis promotes fast cycling and DNA damage, with downstream effects on clonal composition and function</cite><cite id="40466639">p53 and IL‑1/NF‑κB activation drive senescence that restricts clonal diversity and repopulation</cite>.

- Editing modality matters: Compared with Cas9 nucleases, adenine base editing (ABE) can avoid p53 activation and large deletion events after editing HSPCs, thereby minimizing genotoxic consequences of DSBs and preserving clonal diversity and hematologic function in preclinical sickle cell models. <cite id="34079130">Base editing of HSPCs rescued sickle cell disease in mice and avoided p53 activation and larger deletions observed after Cas9 nuclease treatment</cite>. In CAR T cells, ABE also shows reduced activation of p53 and DNA damage response pathways relative to Cas9, with corresponding changes in chromatin accessibility and improved tumor control, reinforcing that avoiding DSBs reduces p53-driven selection effects. <cite id="40324075">ABE editing reduced baseline p53 and DNA damage response activation and improved tumor control compared to Cas9 in CAR T cells</cite>.

# Integrative Model and Implications

Collectively, the data support a model in which Cas9-induced DSBs activate ATM/ATR–Chk2–p53 signaling, imposing immediate checkpoints and genotoxic stress that can eliminate or remodel clonal composition. Concurrently, proliferative stress and ROS accelerate cell-cycle transit, increasing replication-associated damage and biasing selection toward fast-cycling clones. Over time, p53-driven senescence and inflammatory signaling (IL‑1/NF‑κB) consolidate a durable, less diverse clonal landscape that compromises long-term repopulation. Strategies that temper p38–ROS signaling, modulate p53 activity, or adopt non-cleaving editors (e.g., ABE) can mitigate these responses, preserve clonal diversity, and enhance functional persistence of edited HSPCs. <cite id="39536752">A p38–ROS proliferative stress axis and p53-mediated checkpoints drive DNA damage and selection dynamics in edited HSPCs</cite><cite id="40466639">p53 and IL‑1/NF‑κB–mediated senescence restricts repopulation and diversity, mitigated by p53 or IL‑1 inhibition</cite><cite id="34079130">Base editing avoids p53 activation and deletions relative to Cas9 in HSPCs</cite><cite id="32462051">Cas9 editing induces p53-mediated proliferation delay in HSPCs without major off-targets</cite><cite id="40324075">ABE reduces p53/DNA damage pathway activation and improves function compared to Cas9 in blood cells</cite>.

# Practical Considerations for HSPC Editing

- Culture time and activation protocols that enhance editing efficiency can inadvertently amplify p53-driven responses and proliferative stress, reducing clonal diversity and long-term function; optimizing protocols to balance activation with checkpoint tolerance is essential. <cite id="39536752">Shortening culture time mitigates p53 responses and improves reconstitution, but balancing activation is necessary to maintain HDR efficiency</cite>.

- Pharmacologic or genetic dampening of p38, ATM/ATR, or p53 pathways, and anti-inflammatory interventions (e.g., anakinra) may reduce genotoxic selection pressures and improve polyclonal engraftment, though care must be taken to preserve therapeutic editing efficacy. <cite id="39536752">p38 inhibition expands HSCs and improves edited cell persistence and polyclonality</cite><cite id="40466639">Anakinra or transient p53 inhibition mitigates senescence and enhances polyclonal output in edited HSPCs</cite>.

- Where functional correction does not require DSBs, base editing can be preferred to minimize p53 activation and large deletions, preserving clonal diversity and reducing the risk of dominant, deleterious clones. <cite id="34079130">Base editing of HSPCs rescued phenotype while avoiding p53 activation and deletions seen with Cas9</cite>.

# Key Evidence Gaps

Direct, longitudinal single-cell tracking of clonal dynamics in human HSPCs after Cas9 editing across ATM/Chk2/p53 pathway perturbations remains limited in the retrieved literature, and the relative contributions of apoptosis, quiescence, senescence, and proliferation-driven outgrowth to dominant clone emergence need further resolution in primary human systems. Nonetheless, converging data across HSPCs and engineered blood cells identify p53-centered genotoxic stress, proliferative stress/ROS, and inflammatory senescence as principal mechanisms that drive post-editing clonal selection, with noncleaving editors and targeted checkpoint modulation offering practical mitigation strategies. <cite id="39536752">P53-centered checkpoints and proliferative stress are central to post-editing dysfunction and selection</cite><cite id="40466639">p53/IL‑1–NF‑κB senescence reduces diversity and repopulation capacity</cite><cite id="34079130">Avoiding DSBs with base editing reduces p53 activation and deletions</cite><cite id="32462051">p53-mediated proliferation delay is a common outcome of Cas9 editing in HSPCs</cite><cite id="40324075">Noncleaving ABE reduces p53/DNA damage activation and improves function</cite>.
</answer>

This triggers cell-cycle checkpoints, apoptosis, or senescence, and promotes error-prone repair pathways that can yield deletions and chromosomal abnormalities, thereby shaping clonal composition toward cells with advantageous repair outcomes or tolerance of damage. Evidence from HSPCs and other hematologic systems shows that shortening ex vivo culture mitigates p53-mediated DNA damage responses to Cas9-induced DSBs, improving reconstitution, indicating that p53 signaling is a key driver of post-editing dysfunction and selection pressures in HSPCs. <cite id="39536752">Ex vivo activation shortens culture time mitigates the p53-mediated DNA damage response to CRISPR-Cas9-induced DNA double-strand breaks, enhancing reconstitution capacity of edited HSPCs</cite>.

- Proliferation stress, ROS, and checkpoint activation: Ex vivo activation of HSPCs triggers a p38 MAPK–dependent increase in mitogenic reactive oxygen species, accelerating G1/S transition and inducing proliferation-induced DNA damage. This proliferative stress amplifies DSBs and activates p53 pathways, biasing selection toward clones that progress rapidly through the cell cycle despite damage, at the expense of genome integrity. Pharmacologic p38 inhibition delays G1/S, expands quiescent HSCs, and yields edited cells with superior multilineage differentiation, persistence, polyclonal diversity, and preserved genome integrity, directly linking proliferative stress to clonal selection dynamics. <cite id="39536752">Ex vivo activation triggers a p38 MAPK phosphorylation–ROS axis that promotes fast G1/S progression and proliferation-induced DNA damage, and p38 inhibition expands HSCs and improves edited cell persistence and polyclonal repertoire</cite>.

- Senescence and inflammatory signaling downstream of p53: In HSPCs engineered with Cas9/AAV6 via HDR, durable senescence-like responses are observed, driven by p53 and IL‑1/NF‑κB activation. These responses restrict long-term repopulating capacity and reduce clonal diversity, indicating that inflammatory cytokine signaling cooperates with p53 to enforce a senescence program that curbs competitive fitness of edited clones. Temporary p53 inhibition or blocking IL‑1 signaling (e.g., with anakinra) mitigates these responses and improves repopulating capacity and polyclonal output, demonstrating a therapeutic window to reduce p53/IL‑1–mediated selection against edited clones. <cite id="40466639">CRISPR-Cas9/AAV6 editing in HSPCs triggers durable senescence via p53 and IL‑1/NF‑κB activation, limiting repopulation and clonal diversity; transient p53 inhibition or anakinra mitigates senescence and improves repopulating capacity and polyclonality</cite>.

- p53-mediated proliferation delay and off-targets: In patient-derived HSPCs edited for Friedreich ataxia, a p53-mediated proliferation delay is observed without major off-target lesions, consistent with p53-driven growth control being a dominant effect of Cas9 editing. This proliferation delay represents a clonal selection pressure that reduces the expansion of highly damaged or misrepaired cells while allowing survival of cells with tolerable lesions or efficient repair. <cite id="32462051">CRISPR-Cas9 editing of HSPCs from Friedreich ataxia patients induced a p53-mediated proliferation delay in edited cells without major off-target effects</cite>.
